correctness.rationale: The admissible-pair characterization is exactly the finite one-point-extension condition for a poset: transitivity forces downward/upward closure and \(L<U\), and conversely those conditions define a valid extension realized by the random poset. Algebraic types are the parameter equalities. Membership in #P follows from ternary labels. For \(Q_m=P\oplus C_m\), splitting the top-chain status into all-U, an initial incomparable block with no L, and a nonempty L block gives \(c(Q_m)=c(P)+mJ(P)+\binom{m+1}{2}\); subtracting total type counts at \(m=1,2\) recovers \(J(P)\) with two queries, both having greatest elements. The inspected verifier independently checks every naturally labelled poset through five points and the reduction identity for \(m=1,2,3\).

originality.rationale: The lower-set/upper-set description of finite one-point poset extensions is prior, and #P-completeness of counting antichains/ideals is prior. The new content is the explicit top-chain identity that transfers that hardness to finite-parameter random-poset 1-type counts, including the greatest-element promise. Resultary search found only global tuple-orbit profiles of random-poset reducts, a different invariant with no input parameter poset and no counting-complexity statement.

value.rationale: Finite-parameter type counting is a natural quantitative model-theoretic task, and the random poset is a canonical homogeneous structure. The theorem gives an exact combinatorial representation and a sharp counting-complexity barrier, including a strong greatest-element promise, so it is useful beyond a small-instance census.

final_claim: For a finite parameter subposet \(P\) of the countable random poset, nonalgebraic complete 1-types are exactly admissible pairs \((L,U)\) with \(L\) a down-set, \(U\) an up-set, and every \(l\in L\) below every \(u\in U\); exact counting of all 1-types is #P-complete under polynomial-time Turing reductions, even for inputs with a greatest element.
limitations: The hardness is under a two-query polynomial-time Turing reduction, not claimed parsimonious or many-one.
Only exact counting is addressed; no approximation-complexity result or restricted-poset tractability classification is claimed.
